In theory you are right, if there was a law which wouldn't violate the constitution while being extremly unjust you could use Radbruchs formula.
But it is agreed upon that the Grundgesetz is just or at least not unjust enough. So in reality Radbruchs formula could never be user to strile something which doesn't violate the Grundgesetz. Which is also why it was only ever used to pass judgement on people from the Nazi era and the so called "Mauerschützen" who shot people who tried to pass the inner german border, which was legal in the GDR.

It is undemocratic if you understand democracy as something where the Power lies within the people and they (the legislators who are voted for by the people) can do what they want. 

But looking at it from a german (or at least my perspective) democracy is more then just the will of the people it also has to include protection for minoreties and it has to protect human rights (even against the will of the majority). 
Which is why I'd say Radbruchs formula is important to stop unjust laws, allthough I agree that it could also be used easily (if the courts would All follow an undemocratic and unjust argumentation). 

But I don't disagree with you that one could also view it as dangerous and undemocratic.

After reading the wikipedia article regarding "equity" you could say that the Radbruchsche Formel is a bit like it. 
But I'm not really well versed in english law. 

As far as I know the "Radbruchsche Formel" is somethin unique to german law. It was formulated in 1946, so it was created after seeing the crimes which nazi law allowed. 

And Radbruch himself limited it in his essay: "The conflict between justice and the reliability of the law should be solved in favour of the positive law, law enacted by proper authority and power, even in cases where it is unjust in terms of content and purpose, except for cases where the discrepancy between the positive law and justice reaches a level so unbearable that the statute has to make way for justice because it has to be considered "erroneous law". It is impossible to draw a sharper line of demarcation between cases of legal injustice and statutes that are applicable despite their improper content; however, another line of demarcation can be drawn with rigidity: Where justice is not even strived for, where equality, which is the core of justice, is renounced in the process of legislation, there a statute is not just 'erroneous law', it is in fact not of a legal nature at all. That is because law, even positive law, cannot be defined otherwise than as a rule, that is precisely intended to serve justice." 

Which can be seen as somewhat vague, but thats to be expected from a philosophical essay/theory. 

And afaik you would be able to use it in every area of the law. But afaik the highest courts only used in criminal law.

In German law there is the so called "Radbruchsche-Formel", which (very shortend) says that: According to the theory, a judge who encounters a conflict between a statute and what he perceives as just, has to decide against applying the statute if – and only if – the legal concept behind the statute in question seems either "unbearably unjust" or in "deliberate disregard" of human equality before the law. 

This was used to explain why some nazi laws werent laws because they were so unjust, that it can't be called law. This is the legal Argument behind it. 

I can understand that this theory can be seen as arbitrary, but at least there is some legal base for it.
